analysis.title: How the bearish risks can offset each other
key_insights: November has been volatile: the average S&P 500 daily move is 1.2%, the most since April 2025 (Liberation Day tariffs). The 2yr Treasury yield rose 33bps last week, the biggest weekly jump since October 2024.
Three financial stress points eased in recent weeks: oil fell on lower US-Iran escalation fears after the midterms, AI growth fears ebbed, and European fiscal stress eased slightly.
The January Brent contract fell from $113.43/bbl at the end of October to $96.58/bbl at time of writing. Near-term inflation swaps fell on both sides of the Atlantic.
The Philly semiconductor index rose over 12% from its November 5 lows to last Friday's close. IG and HY credit spreads tightened on both sides of the Atlantic over the same period.
The Franco-German 10yr spread fell from a 174bps peak on October 22 to 156bps. Long-end sovereign yields are also below last month's highs.
The S&P 500 posted its first weekly gain after four consecutive declines, and the 10yr Treasury yield had its biggest weekly jump since April 2025.

DB argues the three main bearish risks (higher oil and inflation from Middle East tension, an AI growth slowdown hitting tech and equities, and fiscal stress widening European sovereign spreads) are hard to see occurring together because they offset each other.

An AI growth scare would lower capex and productivity expectations and weaken equities, which would lower government bond yields and ease fiscal concerns. It would also dampen demand-driven inflation in energy and memory chips, make rate hikes less likely and ease front-end yields.
Equity declines tighten financial conditions, which further lowers the chance of rate hikes.

Last week markets priced in more central bank rate hikes, unwinding the dovish repricing that followed the recent financial stress. DB compares this to the 2022-23 hiking cycle, when dovish repricings were repeatedly undone.

Causes of the hawkish repricing: an upside surprise in US CPI (3m annualised core CPI +3.75% in October, fastest since April 2024), no US-Iran deal, and easier financial conditions from the tech recovery and tighter credit spreads.

Markets now price 113bps of Fed hikes by the September 2027 meeting (25bps already delivered plus 88bps ahead). On the day before the last hiking cycle started, markets priced 95bps by the same point in the cycle, so pricing has already passed that.

Markets have tended to underestimate the scale of hiking cycles at the start, and investors have over-weighted the probability of a dovish pivot during financial stress. A pivot is hard while headline and core inflation stay above target, as with SVB in the last cycle.
Easier financial conditions from equity recovery and tighter spreads give central banks more room to prioritise inflation, so hike risk rises again. Hawkish risks have not gone away.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Fastest pace since April 2024. The upside CPI surprise fed fears that inflation is broadening and pushed rate hike pricing higher.
Biggest weekly jump since October 2024, reflecting repricing toward more Fed hikes.
Above the 95bps priced the day before the last hiking cycle began, so markets are already pricing a larger cycle than at that start.
Down from $113.43/bbl at end of October as US-Iran escalation fears faded.
Down from a 174bps peak on October 22, which signals easing European fiscal stress.

risk_factors: Hawkish repricing: easier financial conditions from the equity recovery and tighter spreads give central banks room to focus on inflation, which raises hike odds.
Inflation broadening, shown by the upside US CPI surprise and 3m annualised core CPI of +3.75%.
No US-Iran deal, which could push energy prices back up.
An AI growth slowdown, which would hit tech and equities but also lower yields and inflation pressure.
European fiscal stress, which has eased but could widen spreads again.

tension_points.bull_case: Recovering tech stocks and tighter credit spreads ease financial conditions and show the economy can cope with higher rates, though this lifts hike odds.
tension_points.bear_case: A serious AI growth wobble would hit tech and equities. DB says it would also lower yields, ease fiscal stress, reduce inflation pressure and cut the chance of rate hikes.

tension_points.bull_case: Financial stress could lead central banks to pivot dovish and unwind hike pricing, as happened in the recent repricing.
tension_points.bear_case: With headline and core inflation above target, a dovish pivot is hard, as with the Fed and ECB after SVB. Easier conditions return the focus to inflation and raise hike odds.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI, oil and fiscal risks are hard to see happening at once because an AI scare would lower yields and inflation pressure.
theme_stances.evidence: it would be very hard for all three outcomes to occur simultaneously

theme_stances.key_argument: Easier financial conditions give central banks room to prioritise inflation, and markets have tended to underestimate the size of hiking cycles.
theme_stances.evidence: markets have consistently tended to underestimate the scale of rate hiking cycles at the start
